p.src: Now Zhang Zhao offered a plan: “For the present, we should refrain from mobilizing the army. The moment we raise troops, Cao Cao will surely return. It would be better to write two letters: one to Liu Zhang, saying that Liu Bei has allied with Eastern Wu to seize Western River, so that Liu Zhang will grow suspicious and attack Liu Bei; and another to Zhang Lu, urging him to advance upon Jingzhou, leaving Liu Bei unable to aid both front and rear. Then we may raise our army and take it; the enterprise will succeed.” Sun Quan followed his advice and at once dispatched envoys to both places.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xuande had long remained at Jiameng Pass and had won the people's deep affection. Suddenly he received a letter from Kongming and learned that Lady Sun had returned to Eastern Wu. Hearing also that Cao Cao had raised an army against Ruxu, he consulted Pang Tong: “Cao Cao is attacking Sun Quan. If Cao Cao wins, he will surely seize Jingzhou; if Sun Quan wins, he too will surely seize Jingzhou. What are we to do?” Pang Tong replied, “My lord, do not worry. With Kongming there, I doubt Eastern Wu will dare invade Jingzhou. You may send an urgent letter to Liu Zhang, claiming that Cao Cao has attacked Sun Quan. Say that Sun Quan has appealed to Jingzhou for aid; that we and Sun Quan are neighboring states as close as lips and teeth and cannot refuse assistance; and that Zhang Lu is a bandit concerned only with defending himself and will certainly not dare cross the border. Say that you now wish to muster the army, return to Jingzhou, and join Sun Quan in defeating Cao Cao, but lack troops and provisions. Ask him, in recognition of your kinship, to send quickly thirty or forty thousand picked troops and one hundred thousand hu of provisions, without delay. Once we obtain troops, horses, money, and grain, we can make other plans.”

p.src: Xuande accepted the proposal and sent a messenger to Chengdu. When the messenger reached the pass, Yang Huai and Gao Pei learned of the matter. Gao Pei remained to guard the pass, while Yang Huai accompanied the messenger to Chengdu and presented the letter to Liu Zhang. After reading it, Liu Zhang asked why Yang Huai had come as well. Yang Huai replied, “I came expressly because of this letter. Ever since Liu Bei entered the Riverlands, he has dispensed favors widely to win the people's hearts. His intentions are most sinister. Now that he asks for troops, horses, money, and grain, you must on no account give them to him. To aid him would be to add fuel to the fire.” Liu Zhang said, “Xuande and I share the affection of brothers. How can I refuse to help him?” One man stepped forward and said, “Liu Bei is a formidable hero. To let him remain long in Shu without sending him away is to admit a tiger into one's chamber. If you now give him troops, horses, money, and grain besides, how is that different from adding wings to a tiger?” All looked at the speaker: he was Liu Ba, styled Zichu, a native of Zhengyang in Lingling. On hearing Liu Ba's words, Liu Zhang hesitated, unable to decide. Huang Quan likewise remonstrated earnestly. Liu Zhang therefore allotted only four thousand old and infirm soldiers and ten thousand hu of rice. He sent a letter and envoy in reply to Xuande, while ordering Yang Huai and Gao Pei to guard the passes closely. Liu Zhang's envoy reached Jiameng Pass, met Xuande, and presented the reply. Xuande flew into a rage: “I defend you against your enemy, exhausting my strength and taxing my mind. Yet you begrudge wealth and stint rewards. How can you make the soldiers risk their lives for you?” He tore the reply to pieces, rose, and cursed furiously. The envoy fled back to Chengdu. Pang Tong said, “My lord has always placed benevolence and righteousness above all. By tearing up the letter and venting your anger today, you have cast aside all your former goodwill.” Xuande asked, “If so, what should be done?” Pang Tong replied, “I have three plans. I ask my lord to choose one and act upon it.”

p.src: Xuande asked what the three plans were. Pang Tong said, “Choose picked troops at once, march day and night, and strike directly at Chengdu by surprise. This is the best plan. Yang Huai and Gao Pei are renowned generals of Shu, each commanding strong forces and holding the passes against us. Now, my lord, pretend that you intend to return to Jingzhou. When the two generals hear of it, they will surely come to see you off. At the place of farewell, seize and kill them, take the pass, capture Fu first, and then advance on Chengdu. This is the middle plan. Withdraw to Baidi, return to Jingzhou by night, and slowly devise a later advance. This is the worst plan. If you linger indecisively and do not leave, you will fall into desperate straits beyond rescue.” Xuande said, “Your best plan is too hasty, Strategist, and your worst too slow. The middle plan is neither rushed nor tardy; we shall carry it out.”

Seeing Zhang Song distracted and uneasy, Zhang Su grew suspicious. Zhang Song brought wine and drank with Zhang Su. When I heard of it, I felt as though I had lost something precious. On receiving this letter, advance your troops with all speed. I shall serve as your ally within. By no means bring ruin upon yourself!”

Why have you two conspired to estrange us?” Pang Tong ordered the attendants to search them, and each man was indeed found to be carrying a sharp knife. Pang Tong at once ordered both men beheaded. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan had already seized all two hundred attendants, without letting a single man escape. Xuande summoned them in and gave each wine to calm his fears. Xuande said, “Yang Huai and Gao Pei sought to estrange me from my brother and concealed sharp knives to assassinate me; therefore they were executed. You are innocent, so you need not be alarmed or suspicious.” They all bowed and thanked him. Pang Tong said, “I shall now have you guide us and lead our army to seize the pass. Each of you will be richly rewarded.”

Upon reaching Luo City, they deployed the troops and guarded every strategic pass.
Liu Gui said, “Luo City is Chengdu’s shield. If it is lost, Chengdu will be difficult to defend.
Let the four of us agree that two shall defend the city, while two go forward from Luo City and establish two camps amid the hills and strong terrain, so the enemy cannot approach the walls.”
Leng Bao and Deng Xian said, “We are willing to go and establish the camps.”
Liu Gui was delighted. He divided off twenty thousand troops and gave them to Leng Bao and Deng Xian, who established their camps sixty li from the city.
Liu Gui and Zhang Ren remained to guard Luo City.

p.src: Now that Xuande had taken Fu River Pass, he consulted Pang Tong about advancing on Luo City. A messenger reported that Liu Zhang had dispatched four generals and that Leng Bao and Deng Xian had that very day led twenty thousand troops to establish two large camps sixty li from the city. Xuande assembled his officers and asked, “Who dares win the first distinction by seizing the two generals’ camps?” The veteran general Huang Zhong immediately stepped forward and said, “I am willing to go.” Xuande said, “Lead your own troops toward Luo City, old general. If you capture the camps of Leng Bao and Deng Xian, you shall certainly be richly rewarded.”

Let each of you lead his own troops and attack one camp. p.src: Meanwhile, Huang Zhong returned to camp and gave orders that the men were to cook at the fourth watch the next day, make ready at the fifth, and advance at dawn through the valley on the left. Wei Yan, however, secretly sent a man to discover when Huang Zhong would set out. p.src: On receiving the order, the soldiers ate their fill, removed the bells from their horses, held gags between their teeth, furled their banners, and bound their armor tight before stealing through the darkness to raid the camp. Around the third watch, they left camp and advanced. Halfway there, Wei Yan reflected in the saddle, “Merely attacking Deng Xian’s camp will hardly display my ability. Better first to attack Leng Bao’s camp, then use my victorious troops against Deng Xian’s. The credit for both victories will then be mine.” He immediately passed down an order from horseback that all the soldiers were to take the mountain road on the left. As dawn began to break and Leng Bao’s camp lay not far away, he ordered the soldiers to rest briefly and set their gongs, drums, banners, spears, swords, and other weapons in array.

p.src: But a sentry posted along the road had already raced back to report, and Leng Bao was prepared. At the blast of a cannon, the whole army mounted and charged out. Wei Yan spurred forward with saber in hand and engaged Leng Bao. The two generals crossed horses and fought for thirty bouts, whereupon the troops of Shu divided into two columns and attacked the Han army. The Han troops had marched for half the night, and men and horses alike were exhausted. Unable to withstand the attack, they turned and fled. Hearing his formation collapse behind him, Wei Yan broke off from Leng Bao, wheeled his horse, and fled. The troops of Shu pursued, and the Han army suffered a crushing defeat. Before they had gone five li, drums thundered behind the mountain. Deng Xian led a fierce body of troops out from the valley to bar their way and shouted, “Wei Yan, dismount at once and surrender!”

p.src: Wei Yan urged his horse into a headlong gallop, but it suddenly stumbled, fell to its knees, and threw him to the ground. Deng Xian galloped up and thrust his spear at Wei Yan. Before the spear could strike, a bowstring twanged, and Deng Xian toppled backward from his horse. Leng Bao was just coming up from behind to rescue him when a great general galloped down the hillside and cried in a terrible voice, “The veteran general Huang Zhong is here!” Brandishing his saber, he charged straight at Leng Bao. p.src: Huang Zhong’s force rescued Wei Yan, slew Deng Xian, and pursued the enemy all the way to their camp. Leng Bao wheeled his horse and fought Huang Zhong once more. After scarcely more than ten bouts, the troops behind Huang Zhong surged forward. Leng Bao was forced to abandon the left camp and lead his defeated men toward the right camp. There he saw that all the banners in the camp had changed. Leng Bao was greatly alarmed. Reining in to look, he saw directly ahead a great general in golden armor and a brocade robe: it was Liu Xuande, with Liu Feng on his left and Guan Ping on his right. They shouted, “We have already taken your camp. Where do you think you are going?” Xuande had in fact led troops up from the rear in support and seized Deng Xian’s camp while the opportunity offered.

p.src: With both ways blocked, Leng Bao took a secluded mountain path in an attempt to return to Luo City. Before he had gone ten li, ambushers suddenly rose on the narrow path. They thrust out their hooked poles together and captured Leng Bao alive. It was Wei Yan. Knowing that he had broken military law and had no excuse, he had rallied the rear guard, made soldiers of Shu guide him, and laid an ambush there. Leng Bao had come straight into the trap. p.src: Meanwhile, Xuande raised a banner promising immunity from death and forbade anyone to harm any soldier of Shu who reversed his spear and cast off his armor; whoever injured one would pay with his life. He further proclaimed to the surrendered soldiers, “All you men of Shu have parents, wives, and children. Those willing to submit may join my army; those unwilling will be released to return home.” At this, cheers shook the earth. After establishing his camp, Huang Zhong went directly to Xuande and said that Wei Yan had disobeyed military orders and deserved execution. Xuande promptly summoned Wei Yan, who arrived escorting Leng Bao. Xuande said, “Though Yan is guilty, this achievement may redeem his offense.” He ordered Wei Yan to thank Huang Zhong for saving his life and forbade the two men from contending with each other thereafter. Wei Yan bowed his head to the ground and confessed his fault. Xuande richly rewarded Huang Zhong. He had Leng Bao brought under guard before his tent, removed his bonds, and gave him wine to calm his fright. Then he asked, “Will you surrender?” Leng Bao replied, “Since you have spared my life, how could I refuse to surrender? Liu Gui, Zhang Ren, and I are sworn friends unto death. If you will release me, I shall immediately persuade them both to surrender and deliver Luo City to you.” Xuande was delighted. He bestowed clothing, a saddle, and a horse upon Leng Bao and ordered him to return to Luo City. Wei Yan said, “This man must not be released. Once he escapes, he will never return.” Xuande replied, “I treat others with benevolence and righteousness; they will not betray me.”

p.src: Now Leng Bao returned to Luo City and met Liu Gui and Zhang Ren. He said nothing of his capture and release, but claimed instead, “I killed more than ten of them, seized a horse, and escaped.” Liu Gui hurriedly sent a man to Chengdu to request aid. p.src: Wu Yi recommended Wu Lan and Lei Tong as deputy generals, mustered twenty thousand troops, and came to Luo City. Liu Gui and Zhang Ren received him and related all that had happened. Wu Yi said, “With the enemy at the city walls, it will be difficult to resist them. What sound plans do you have?” Leng Bao said, “This whole region lies close beside the Fu River, whose current is very swift. The enemy camp ahead occupies the foot of the mountain, the lowest ground there. Grant me five thousand troops, each carrying spades and hoes, and I will breach the banks of the Fu River and drown Liu Bei’s entire army.” Wu Yi adopted his plan and immediately ordered Leng Bao to go and release the waters, while Wu Lan and Lei Tong led troops in support. Leng Bao accepted the order and went off to prepare the tools needed to breach the riverbank.

p.src: Pang Tong withdrew to his lodgings, where a gatekeeper suddenly reported, “A visitor has come expressly to see you.” Pang Tong went out to receive him and saw a man eight chi tall and remarkably imposing in appearance.
